facts: Hermitage is a northern Rhône appellation that produces mostly red wine from Syrah, with small amounts of white from Marsanne and Roussanne.
Appellation rules allow Syrah to be topped up with 15% or less of Marsanne and/or Roussanne.
Because of their high tannin, the reds are usually aged longer than American or Australian Syrahs and are often cellared up to 40 years.
Vin de paille, or straw wine, is also produced in the region.
In the Banyuls Grand Cru AOC, the wine is required to be aged in wood barrels for two and a half years.
Crémant de Limoux uses the traditional method.
The Upper Loire has Sauvignon blanc in Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, and the Lower Loire reaches the Atlantic through Muscadet, where Melon de Bourgogne dominates.
The Middle Loire, around Touraine, Saumur, Chinon and Vouvray, is dominated by Chenin blanc and Cabernet franc.
Most production is white wine from Chenin blanc, Sauvignon blanc and Melon de Bourgogne, with red wines from Cabernet franc, especially around Chinon.
Because of the marginal climate, vintage quality has a bigger effect on Loire wines than on those of other French wine regions.
With Crémant production throughout the Loire, it is the second largest sparkling wine producer in France after Champagne.
Margaux has 21 cru classé châteaux, more than any other commune in Bordeaux, including the first growth Château Margaux.
The appellation includes the villages of Margaux, Cantenac, Arsac, Soussans and Labarde.
The soil is the thinnest in the Médoc, with the highest proportion of gravel, which gives good drainage.
Cabernet Sauvignon is the predominant grape, always blended with others, and the wines are known for their perfumed fragrance and blackcurrant fruit.
Wine from the southern part of the appellation tends to be more powerful but less fragrant, leaning towards plum.
Médoc AOC covers the northern third of the Médoc peninsula on the Left Bank of the Gironde estuary, and is the area once called Bas-Médoc.
Soils are Garonne gravel, Pyrenees gravel and clayey limestone, and heavy clay-rich areas suit Merlot better than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are the main grapes, with Petit Verdot, Malbec, Cabernet Franc and Carménère also allowed.
It is mostly an area of cooperatives, and none of its estates were included in the 1855 Bordeaux classification.
Meursault is a Côte de Beaune commune in Burgundy, and white wine from Chardonnay makes up around 98% of production.
There are no Grand Cru vineyards within Meursault, but there are several Premier Cru vineyards.
White Meursault typically shows clear oak influence and malolactic fermentation, which leads to descriptions such as buttery.
Premier Cru climats lie in two groups, north of the village bordering Volnay and a larger group to the south toward Puligny-Montrachet and Blagny.
Muscadet is made in the Pays Nantais at the western end of the Loire Valley, from the Melon de Bourgogne grape alone.
Muscadet-Sèvre et Maine is the most productive sub-appellation, making more than three-quarters of the region's production, and it takes its name from the rivers Sèvre and Maine.
Sur lie ageing means the wine stays in contact with the lees after fermentation, which gives a creamier mouthfeel and a fuller body.
The generic Muscadet AOC cannot use sur lie, but the three sub-appellations can.
Pauillac includes three of the five premier cru châteaux of Bordeaux: Latour, Lafite Rothschild and Mouton Rothschild.
It sits on the Left Bank of the Gironde within the Haut-Médoc, between St-Julien to the south and St-Estèphe to the north.
The soil is gravelly, and the forest to the west shelters the vines from the Atlantic winds.
Cabernet Sauvignon is the predominant grape, always blended with other grapes such as Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carménère.
The style has been described as stark, with blackcurrant fruit and pencil-shavings and cigar-box notes.
The appellation was created in 1987, and before then the area was part of the Graves AOC.
It lies in the northern part of Graves, on the left bank of the Garonne, immediately south of the city of Bordeaux.
It includes Château Haut-Brion, the only red-wine producer outside the Haut-Médoc classified in the 1855 classification, and all the châteaux in the 1953/59 Graves classification.
Red wines are led by Cabernet Sauvignon with somewhat more Merlot than in the Médoc, while dry whites blend Sauvignon blanc and Sémillon.
The soil is very gravelly, and the white wines are typically fermented in barrels at a low temperature.
Pomerol is a Right Bank appellation in the Libournais, and its wine is predominately Merlot with Cabernet Franc in a supporting role.
There is no official classification of Pomerol wine, though Château Pétrus is widely held to be equivalent to premier cru.
The sub-soil is dark packed clay with a high iron content, and the plateau stands on a gravel bank.
Pomerol is the smallest of the major fine wine regions in Bordeaux, and almost all the wine is estate-bottled.
The AOC rules from 1936 outlawed plantings of any white grape varieties.
The wine will typically receive 18 to 20 months of aging in barriques prior to bottling and release.
Provence has nine AOCs, and Côtes de Provence is the largest, followed by Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence and Coteaux Varois en Provence.
Red Bandol must age at least 18 months in oak before release and usually needs at least 10 years of aging to develop fully.
The strong mistral wind from the north cools and dries the grapes, but it can damage vines that are not securely trained.
Cassis AOC is unusual in Provence because white wine makes up over 75% of its production.
Puligny-Montrachet is a Côte de Beaune commune in Burgundy, and around 99.5% of its production is white wine.
There are four Grand Cru vineyards: Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet and Chevalier-Montrachet.
Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet cross the communal border and are shared with Chassagne-Montrachet.
The Premier Cru climats lie both south of the village toward Chassagne-Montrachet and north toward Meursault.
White Puligny-Montrachet is often very mineral, with more restrained oak than some other Côte de Beaune villages, and is usually described as elegant.
The Rhône is generally divided into the Northern Rhône and the Southern Rhône, each with distinct vinicultural traditions.
In the Northern Rhône, Syrah is the only red grape permitted, and whites come from Marsanne, Roussanne and Viognier.
The northern Rhône has a continental climate with harsh winters and warm summers, and the mistral brings colder air from the Massif Central.
In parts of the south, Châteauneuf-du-Pape best known, large pebbles around the vine bases absorb the sun's heat by day and keep the vines warm at night.
